newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Sweden's Asbrink sees possible risks in EMU.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Asbrink sees possible risks in EMU.

text.p: Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said on Monday he sees potential risks involved in the European Union's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), questioning whether the bloc is an "optimal currency area."

Asbrink, speaking just days after the executive committee of his ruling Social Democrats said Sweden would not join EMU from the start, said there would in some respects be "limited adjustment mechanisms" when there was a common monetary policy.
He specifically referred to low wage flexibility and geographical mobility in the EU, saying that it was there that he saw a big risk.

"What I see as a problem or risk is to create a common currency for a number of countries which are to such an extent different in terms of industry structure and in terms of degree of (economic) development," Asbrink told reporters late on Sunday.
"Is the EU an optimal currency area?" he asked.
A country which did not join EMU and held on to its currency and monetary policy would keep such an adjustment mechanism.
Asked whether he meant the possibility of devaluing, he said: "Yes, you could say that. (But) you can just as well say the possibility to revalue."

Asbrink later rejected the interpretation of his remarks that one reason for Sweden not to join EMU in 1999 was the possibility to devalue its currency. "No, it is not. I don't have that view," he told Reuters. "I'm not a supporter of devaluations."
Outside EMU, Sweden would need to pursue an economic policy which was just as strict, if not stricter, and such a policy would not lead to a weaker crown, rather the opposite, he said.
Asbrink said the lack of popular support for EMU had been a decisive factor in the decision of the party committee to decide against membership from the start in 1999.

That decision is virtually certain to be confirmed by an extraordinary party congress in September and later this year by parliament. But the party board left the door open to join at a later date. -- Brussels newsroom +32 2 287 68 11
